newsitem.title: USA: Freshman Rep. Stockman unseated in Texas run-off.
newsitem.headline: Freshman Rep. Stockman unseated in Texas run-off.

text.p: Freshman Republican Representative Steve Stockman, swept into office in the 1994 mid-term elections, was unseated in one of three run-off races held in Texas Tuesday to fill the remaining seats in the U.S. House.

Texas voters also sent Democratic incumbent Ken Bentsen back to Washington for a second term and elected Republican Kevin Brady to fill a seat vacated by retiring Representative Jack Fields in a district in the northern Houston suburbs.

The run-off elections were called after no candidates won majorities in the districts, among 13 redrawn after a federal court panel ruled that two districts in Houston and one in Dallas had been racially gerrymandered.

Stockman, dubbed "Congressman Clueless" by a Texas magazine and criticised for close ties to rightwing militia groups after the Oklahoma City bombing, conceded to Democratic challenger Nick Lampson trailing 53-47 percent.

Lampson staked his claim to the 9th district seat with strong support from labour unions in Jefferson County, a heavily industrialised area along the Louisiana border dotted with oil refineries and chemical plants.
"This was purely mechanics," Stockman said. "We said in the beginning that what mattered was who got the votes out. They got 56,000 votes out. That's a tremendous amount."

The Justice Department sent 24 federal observers to monitor polls and vote-counting in Jefferson and Galveston counties after uncovering evidence minority voters were harassed in early voting last week by Stockman supporters.
"It's been a bloody, bloody battle," Tom Pauken, Texas Republican state chairman, said of the Stockman-Lampson race.

Voting in the three congressional races was light, with a fraction of the eligible voters in the Houston-area districts turning out. "I've been estimating a 10 percent turnout, including early voting," said Harris County Clerk Beverly Kaufman. "It's just been so quiet."
In the 25th district in southeast Houston, Bentsen was sent back to Washington by a 57-43 percent margin with 97 percent of the precincts reporting.

"We ran a strong campaign talking about the issues people wanted to hear about, like you did, and I think that's what put us over the top," Bentsen said in a telephone conversation with President Clinton.

Bentsen's Republican challenger, Dolly Madison McKenna, was seemingly unable to overcome strong opposition from the religious right angered over her pro-choice stand on abortion, political analysts said.

Anti-abortion groups were encouraging voters to file blank ballots in the special election to protest the abortion-rights positions of McKenna and incumbent Bentsen, nephew of former U.S. Sen. and Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen.

Republicans were assured of holding onto their seat in the 8th district, where two Republicans -- state Representative Kevin Brady and physician Gene Fontenot -- squared off for the fourth time this year.

Fontenot trailed in the March primary and lost a party run-off, and despite pouring more than $1 million of his own money into the race trailed Brady in the court-ordered November primary before losing in today's run-off 59-41 percent with 99 percent of the precincts reporting.
"You won because integrity matters. You won because you care about and I care about our communities," Brady told campaign supporters celebrating the victory.

With the Bentsen and Lampson wins, Democrats held their slim majority in the Texas congressional delegation. The races were not a threat to the Republican party's majority in the House, but trimmed it by two seats to 227-207.
